notes.definition: Most electrical appliances are connected to the mains with a three-core cable. The live wire (brown) carries the alternating potential difference from the supply, the neutral wire (blue) completes the circuit, and the earth wire (green and yellow stripes) is a safety wire that stops the appliance's casing becoming live.
explanation: Most mains appliances are connected by a three-core cable. Each of the three wires, or cores, is a copper conductor covered in plastic insulation of a different colour, so that it can be identified. The three cores are wrapped together in an outer layer of plastic insulation. Copper is used because it is a good electrical conductor; plastic is used because it is a good insulator.

The live wire has brown insulation. It carries the alternating potential difference from the supply. The neutral wire has blue insulation and completes the circuit, carrying current back from the appliance. The earth wire has green and yellow stripes. It is a safety wire, connected to the metal casing of the appliance, that stops the casing becoming live if a fault occurs.

The potential difference between the live wire and earth is about 230 V. The neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V). The earth wire is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault, for example if a loose live wire touches the metal casing. Then a current flows through the earth wire to the ground instead of through a person who touches the casing.

The human body is at earth potential (0 V). If you touch the live wire, there is a large potential difference of about 230 V across your body. This causes a current to flow through your body to earth, giving an electric shock that can burn you, stop your heart and kill you. This is why the live wire can be dangerous even when a switch in the circuit is open: the switch breaks the circuit, but the live wire before the switch is still at 230 V, so touching it would still give a shock.

Any connection between the live wire and earth is dangerous. Because there is a large potential difference and very little resistance, a very large current flows. This could heat wires enough to melt insulation and start a fire. If the connection is through a person, the current through their body could be fatal. Damaged cables, frayed insulation, water in sockets and metal objects poked into sockets can all create such a connection.
keyFacts: Most appliances are connected to the mains by a three-core cable.
Live wire: brown; carries the alternating potential difference from the supply.
Neutral wire: blue; completes the circuit; at or close to 0 V.
Earth wire: green and yellow stripes; safety wire to stop the casing becoming live.
Potential difference between live and earth is about 230 V.
The earth wire is at 0 V and only carries a current if there is a fault.
Your body is at earth potential, so touching the live wire puts about 230 V across you.
A live wire can be dangerous even when a switch in the circuit is open.
A connection between live and earth gives a large current: risk of shock and fire.

keyTerms.definition: A cable with three insulated copper wires (live, neutral and earth) inside an outer insulating layer.
The brown wire that carries the alternating potential difference (about 230 V) from the supply.
The blue wire that completes the circuit; it is at or close to earth potential (0 V).
The green and yellow striped safety wire, at 0 V, that stops an appliance's casing becoming live; it carries current only when there is a fault.
A potential of 0 V, the potential of the ground and of a person standing on it.
Plastic covering on wires that does not conduct electricity, preventing contact with the conductor.

workedExamples.title: Why is touching the live wire dangerous?
workedExamples.question: Explain why a person who touches the live wire of a mains circuit gets an electric shock.
steps: The live wire is at a potential of about 230 V.
The person's body is at earth potential, 0 V.
So there is a potential difference of about 230 V across the body.
This drives a current through the body to earth, which is the electric shock.
workedExamples.answer: A 230 V potential difference across the body drives a current through it to earth.

workedExamples.title: The earth wire in a fault
workedExamples.question: A loose live wire touches the metal case of a washing machine. Explain how the earth wire protects someone who then touches the case.
steps: The earth wire connects the metal case to the ground at 0 V.
When the live wire touches the case, current flows from the live wire through the case and down the earth wire.
The earth wire has a very low resistance, so the current takes this path rather than through the person.
The case is kept at (or near) 0 V, so there is little potential difference across the person.
workedExamples.answer: Current flows safely to earth through the earth wire instead of through the person.

workedExamples.title: Switched off but still dangerous
workedExamples.question: A ceiling light is switched off. An electrician says the live wire in the light fitting can still be dangerous. Explain why.
steps: The switch only breaks the circuit at one point.
The live wire between the supply and the switch is still connected to the 230 V supply.
Your body is at 0 V, so touching it still puts a large potential difference across you.
Current would flow through you to earth, giving a shock. This is why the supply is turned off at the consumer unit before working on wiring.
workedExamples.answer: The live wire can still be at 230 V, so touching it can drive a current through your body to earth.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the neutral wire is the safety wire.
misconceptions.right: In fact the earth wire (green and yellow) is the safety wire. The neutral wire (blue) completes the circuit and normally carries current.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the earth wire carries current all the time.
misconceptions.right: In fact the earth wire only carries a current if there is a fault.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a circuit is completely safe once the switch is off.
misconceptions.right: In fact the live wire can still be at 230 V, so touching it can still cause a shock.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a shock happens because of the potential of the live wire alone.
misconceptions.right: In fact a shock happens because of the potential difference between the live wire (230 V) and your body (0 V), which drives a current through you.

realWorld: Electricians turn off the supply at the consumer unit, not just at a light switch, before working on wiring.
Metal-cased appliances such as washing machines, kettles and toasters have an earth wire connected to the casing.
Cable insulation colours are standardised (brown, blue, green and yellow) so that anyone wiring a plug or appliance connects it safely.
examTips: Learn the colour and job of each wire as a set: live brown (carries the pd), neutral blue (completes the circuit), earth green and yellow (safety).
Give the potentials: live about 230 V, neutral about 0 V, earth 0 V.
When explaining a shock, use the chain: live at 230 V, body at 0 V, large potential difference across body, current flows through body to earth.
When asked about a live-to-earth connection, mention both the risk of shock and the large current that can cause overheating and fire.
summary: Appliances connect to the mains with three-core cable.
Live (brown) carries the alternating pd; neutral (blue) completes the circuit; earth (green and yellow) is for safety.
Live is at about 230 V relative to earth; neutral and earth are at about 0 V.
The earth wire only carries a current when there is a fault.
Touching the live wire puts 230 V across your body, causing a current and a shock.
Connecting live to earth causes a large, dangerous current.

questions.question: What colour is the insulation on the live wire?
markScheme: 1 mark: Brown
questions.explanation: The live wire is brown. Blue is neutral, green and yellow is earth. Black was the old neutral colour.

questions.question: What colour is the insulation on the neutral wire?
markScheme: 1 mark: Blue
questions.explanation: The neutral wire is blue. Red was the old live colour, so do not use it.

questions.question: Which wire is the safety wire that stops an appliance's casing becoming live?
markScheme: 1 mark: Earth
questions.explanation: The earth wire, with green and yellow stripes, is the safety wire.

questions.question: What is the potential difference between the live wire and earth in UK mains?
markScheme: 1 mark: about 230 V
questions.explanation: The live wire is at about 230 V relative to earth. 50 is the frequency in hertz.

questions.question: What is the potential of the neutral wire?
markScheme: 1 mark: At or close to 0 V
questions.explanation: The neutral wire is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V). It is the live wire whose potential alternates.
options: It alternates between +230 V and −230 V

questions.question: When does the earth wire carry a current?
markScheme: 1 mark: Only when there is a fault
questions.explanation: Normally no current flows in the earth wire. It carries current only if a fault connects the live wire to the casing.
options: Only when there is a fault
Only when the appliance is switched off
All the time the appliance is on
Only when the neutral wire is broken

questions.question: What does the neutral wire do?
markScheme: 1 mark: It completes the circuit.
questions.explanation: The neutral wire completes the circuit, taking current back from the appliance. The live wire carries the pd; the earth wire is for safety.
options: It carries the alternating pd from the supply.
It stops the casing becoming live.

questions.question: Why does a person who touches a live wire get an electric shock?
markScheme: 1 mark: There is a large potential difference between the live wire and the body, so current flows through the body.
questions.explanation: The body is at earth potential (0 V) and the live wire is at about 230 V, so a large pd drives a current through the body.
options: The live wire is at 0 V and the body is at 230 V.
There is a large potential difference between the live wire and the body, so current flows through the body.
The live wire stores charge which jumps into the body.
The neutral wire pushes charge through the body.

questions.question: A light switch is open. Which statement is correct?
markScheme: 1 mark: The live wire before the switch can still be at 230 V.
questions.explanation: Opening a switch breaks the circuit, but any part of the live wire still connected to the supply is still at about 230 V.
options: All the wires in the circuit are at 0 V.
The earth wire is now at 230 V.
The live wire before the switch can still be at 230 V.
The neutral wire is now at 230 V.

questions.question: Why is a connection between the live wire and the earth wire dangerous?
markScheme: 1 mark: It makes a very large current flow, which can cause overheating and fire.
questions.explanation: There is a 230 V pd and very little resistance, so a huge current flows, which can heat the wires and start a fire, or cause a shock.
options: It makes a very large current flow, which can cause overheating and fire.
It reverses the direction of the alternating current.
It reduces the potential difference to zero everywhere in the house.

questions.question: Name the three wires in a three-core cable and give the colour of each.
markScheme: 1 mark: live: brown
1 mark: neutral: blue
1 mark: earth: green and yellow stripes
questions.explanation: All three colours are standard throughout the UK and Europe.

questions.question: State the function of the live wire.
markScheme: 1 mark: carries the alternating potential difference from the supply
questions.explanation: The live wire is the one at about 230 V.
acceptedAnswers: carries the alternating potential difference from the supply

questions.question: State the function of the earth wire.
markScheme: 1 mark: a safety wire to stop the appliance (casing) becoming live
questions.explanation: If a fault occurs, current flows to earth through this wire rather than through a person.

questions.question: Explain why the wires in a cable are made of copper and covered in plastic.
markScheme: 1 mark: copper is a good (electrical) conductor
1 mark: plastic is a good insulator, so prevents electric shock / prevents wires touching
questions.explanation: The conductor carries the current; the insulator stops it reaching people or other wires.

questions.question: Explain why touching the live wire can be fatal even though the person is not touching the neutral wire.
markScheme: 1 mark: the body is at earth potential (0 V)
1 mark: so there is a large potential difference (about 230 V) between the live wire and the body
1 mark: so a current flows through the body to earth
questions.explanation: You do not need to touch the neutral wire: the ground completes the path. The pd between live and earth drives the current through you.

questions.question: A metal kettle has a fault: the live wire has come loose and is touching the metal case. Explain how the earth wire keeps the user safe.
markScheme: 1 mark: the earth wire connects the case to earth
1 mark: current flows through the earth wire (low resistance path) to the ground rather than through the user
1 mark: so the case stays at (near) 0 V
questions.explanation: The earth wire provides an easy path to the ground, so a person touching the case is not the path for the current.

questions.question: Suggest why the earth wire is not needed in normal operation of an appliance.
markScheme: 1 mark: in normal use the live and neutral wires complete the circuit, so no current flows in the earth wire
questions.explanation: The circuit is live → appliance → neutral. The earth wire only matters when something goes wrong.

questions.question: Explain why it is dangerous to poke a metal object into a mains socket.
markScheme: 1 mark: metal is a conductor and could touch the live contact (at 230 V)
1 mark: the person is at 0 V, so current would flow through the object and the person to earth (shock)
questions.explanation: The metal provides a path from the live contact through the person to earth.

questions.question: An electrician turns off a light switch before replacing a light fitting. Explain why this is not enough to make the job safe and state what the electrician should do instead.
markScheme: 1 mark: parts of the live wire may still be connected to the supply / at 230 V
1 mark: touching them would put a large pd across the body causing a current/shock
1 mark: switch off the supply to that circuit at the consumer unit (fuse box) before starting
questions.explanation: A switch only breaks the circuit at one point. Turning off the supply at the consumer unit disconnects the whole circuit.
acceptedAnswers: turn off at the consumer unit

questions.question: A student says 'the neutral wire is at 230 V because it carries current'. Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: the neutral wire is at (or close to) 0 V / earth potential
1 mark: current flows because of the potential difference between live and neutral, not because the neutral wire has a high potential
questions.explanation: Current flows from high to low potential; the neutral wire is the low-potential side of the circuit.
acceptedAnswers: current can flow at low potential

questions.question: Describe the three wires in a three-core mains cable. For each wire, give its colour, its potential, its function, and explain when it carries a current.
markScheme: Indicative content: live wire: brown; potential alternates, about 230 V relative to earth; carries the alternating pd from the supply; carries current whenever the appliance is on. Neutral wire: blue; at or close to 0 V (earth potential); completes the circuit; carries current whenever the appliance is on. Earth wire: green and yellow stripes; at 0 V; safety wire connected to metal casing to stop it becoming live; carries current only if there is a fault (e.g. live wire touching casing). All are copper conductors covered in plastic insulation.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three wires described accurately with colour, potential, function and when current flows.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): most features correct for at least two wires, or all wires with some errors or omissions.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct colours or functions.
questions.explanation: The full answer is effectively a table: colour, potential, job, current. Learning it as a table helps you remember it.

questions.question: Explain why a live wire may be dangerous even when a switch in the circuit is open, and explain the dangers of providing any connection between the live wire and earth.
markScheme: Indicative content: the live wire is at about 230 V; an open switch breaks the circuit but the live wire between the supply and the switch is still at 230 V; the human body is at earth potential 0 V; touching the live wire produces a large potential difference across the body; current flows through the body to earth: electric shock, which can be fatal; any connection between live and earth (through a person, a damaged cable, water or a metal object) has a large pd and low resistance; a very large current flows; this can cause overheating, melting insulation and fire, or a fatal shock.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation of both parts using the idea of potential difference between live (230 V) and earth (0 V) driving a current.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as 'you can still get a shock' or 'it can cause a fire', with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Both parts rest on one idea: the live wire is at about 230 V relative to earth, so any path to earth gives a large current.

questions.question: Which wire is connected to the metal case of an appliance?
markScheme: 1 mark: Earth
questions.explanation: The earth wire is connected to the metal casing so that if a fault makes the case live, the current flows safely to earth.

questions.question: Which pair of wires normally carry the current to and from an appliance when it is working?
markScheme: 1 mark: Live and neutral
questions.explanation: The circuit is completed by the live and neutral wires. The earth wire carries current only during a fault.

questions.question: The earth wire in a metal toaster has become disconnected. A fault then connects the live wire to the metal case. What happens when someone touches the case?
markScheme: 1 mark: The case is at about 230 V, so a current flows through the person to earth
questions.explanation: Without the earth wire there is no safe path to the ground. The case is at the live potential, so the person becomes the path to earth and gets a shock.
options: Nothing, because the neutral wire protects them
The case is at about 230 V, so a current flows through the person to earth
The case is at 0 V, so they are safe
The toaster stops working and the case stays safe

questions.question: State the approximate potential difference between: (a) the live wire and the neutral wire; (b) the neutral wire and earth; (c) the live wire and earth.
markScheme: 1 mark: (a) about 230 V
1 mark: (b) about 0 V
1 mark: (c) about 230 V
questions.explanation: Neutral and earth are both at about 0 V, so the live wire is about 230 V from either of them, and there is almost no pd between neutral and earth.

questions.question: The outer insulation of a cable is damaged and the brown wire inside is exposed. What is the main hazard?
markScheme: 1 mark: Someone touching the exposed live wire could get an electric shock
questions.explanation: The brown wire is live, at about 230 V. Touching it puts a large pd across the body, so current flows through the person.
options: The neutral wire could give a shock
The appliance will run on d.c.
Someone touching the exposed live wire could get an electric shock
The earth wire will stop working
